I am a 33-year-old farmer in Quzhou County. My family has about 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. I have a middle school education, and I learned farming from my father and from watching what works in our village. I am not going to gamble with fancy crops — I know the wheat–maize double-cropping system puts food on the table and pays the school fees.

My winter wheat is already in the ground from last October, but it is the start of the real growing season now. I will manage the wheat through to harvest in early June, then immediately plant summer maize on all 8 mu. That is what everyone around here does, and the machines and seed dealers are set up for it. I will buy improved wheat seed — varieties like the ones my neighbors use — and hybrid maize seed, because the hybrids give me the best yield on our land. For wheat I rotary till before sowing; for maize I will sow no-till right after the wheat combine leaves the field, so I do not lose any days of the short summer season.

For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer as a base dressing and top-dress with urea. For the wheat I use a bit more nitrogen because it needs it for the grain, and for maize I make sure it gets enough feed during the rapid growth in July and August. I irrigate the wheat three or four times — the green-up water, the jointing water, and the grain-filling water are the most important. The maize only needs two good irrigations, usually at the jointing and big-flare stages, because the summer rains help. I spray pesticides when I see pests or weeds; usually that means about four times for wheat and three to four times for maize, including herbicide, insecticide, and one fungicide on the wheat.

I expect about 500 kg per mu of wheat and about 550 kg per mu of maize if the weather is normal. That gives me a safe income and enough grain for the family.
